title: Rohatsu 2009
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett emphasizes the importance of letting go of control and trying to organize one's mind during a sesshin experience, instead trusting that everything will unfold naturally. They encourage practitioners to focus on touching the heart of the matter, rather than getting caught up in thoughts or distractions. By doing so, they can find freedom from suffering and cultivate greater understanding, compassion, and awareness.
topics: cyclical view of history and lineage

sentences.text: A tremendous number of conditions have to be present to have a sesshin that feels like sesshin, whatever that is supposed to feel like, but it does.
We have to have some kind of tradition that we have enough faith in to work with, tweak, and interpret in many ways that we have to.
If we didn't start from that, how many committee meetings would it take to figure this out?
We'd have a zendo protocol committee, a meal form committee, and a signals subcommittee.
So that seems like an important condition that is somehow present.

But also, we need the condition of having all of us here and having, it seems, to be essential to have people who have practiced for quite a while, some of whom have been to many sesshin, and also to have people who haven't been to so many sesshin; this also seems to be important.
We need a place to do it and a quiet day, a long list.
I'm really quite amazed and quite grateful that we get to do this together.
The word sesshin, usually at the orientation in English-speaking zendos, they tell you the word sesshin, which is formed of two characters.
The first is actually *sets*.
The 't' gets dropped when it gets combined, I guess.
*Sets*, S-E-T-S-U.
And the second is *shin*, S-H-I-N, which we see in a lot of things.
So *shin* means heart or mind.
They use the same word, not the heart, the pump, but the metaphorical heart, the heart of the matter, the heart of our life.
In Western languages, we sort of privilege the intellect, right?
So we put the mind off in its own word, but in Asian cultures, it's the same word, *shin*.
They always tell you that *sets* means gather, to gather the mind.
So that makes some kind of sense, right?
We feel scattered, so we better take some time and sort of like pull things back together into this little package.
At Lun Lake, said *shin*, when she was doing the orientation, Kate said, who knows enough Japanese to look things up?
She said she finally looked this up.
She was always a little suspicious of that; it didn't sound right.
She looked it up and it turns out to be wrong.
I don't know how many thousands of English-speaking zendos they've told you it means that, but now we know a new thing.
She says it means to touch, which actually makes a lot more sense if you think about it.
Because what is there really to gather?
How would you...
It was lovely the way Bob added a new form if you weren't here during the Rohatsu ceremony.
These flowers sort of just appeared, like from Tushita heaven, I think, is where they come from.
So we had a little temple cleaning time and Bob introduced the form of...
For the cleaning, we picked up the flowers one by one by hand very mindfully.
So that you can gather flowers, I suppose, but how do you gather the mind?
How do you gather the heart?

Maybe we can forget about trying to gather anything, a little bit more just let the chips fall where they may, not to carry control all these funny aspects and facets of personality, of mind, of our being, not try to gather them or control them or organize them or improve them at all.
Just leave them alone and reach right through them and touch the heart of the matter, touch the center of our life instead.
And trust that all those things we're trying to gather will sort themselves out without our interference, without our super smart attempt to organize them.
Because we know how that works out, right?
It's interesting having this tradition that comes through Japan because we have all of these sort of layers of language and meaning.
In a way, they're like these little treasures waiting to be discovered.
So now, 50 years into the American Zen experiment, we discovered this little treasure that we're holding all this time of sesshin to touch the mind.
But there's lots more.
We could go on just about a few words for the whole talk easily.
Like *shin*, for instance, turns out to be the Japanese way of saying the Chinese way of saying a Chinese character.
But in everyday Japanese, you wouldn't say *shin*; you say *kokoro*.
How they got from the Chinese something like *jin* to *shin* is not too big of a leap, but then how do they get to *kokoro*?
Some whole other story full of meaning, I'm sure.
Likewise, when we chanted the names of the Zen ancestors in the ceremony, which is usually in sort of formal Soto Zen temples in Japan, that would be done every morning.
But here we just do it once a year for various reasons.
That's also the Japanese way of saying, you know, Sanskrit and Pali and Chinese names.
And now here we are trying to pronounce it.
Probably if somebody walked in here from Japan, they have no idea what we're talking about.
That's all right; that's what we received.
Just like gathering the mind, we don't need to straighten it all out.
We can just work with it, tweaking a little bit.
So likewise, Rohatsu has a meaning, but it has a pretty pedestrian meaning, it turns out.
*Ro* means the twelfth month of the year.
And *Hatsu* is just the number eight.
So the Buddha's enlightenment is celebrated on the eighth day of the twelfth month.
In Japan, that would have been a lunar, on the lunar calendar in China.
In Japan, towards the end of the eighteenth century, they did this high-speed modernization and westernization.
They switched the Gregorian calendar.
So now we celebrate it on the eighth of December.
But of course, it isn't actually the eighth of December, is it?
It's the fifth of December.
So we are also accommodating the weekday schedule.
Maybe we couldn't all take what would that be, Tuesday or Wednesday?
Maybe we couldn't take that day off and sit all day.
There are many layers of story and meaning here.
All of it, I suppose, is to some extent made up.

But it seems to be a fact of the human sort of cultural and mythological mind that if you make something up, and we all believe in it and put some energy into it, it becomes very real and very important.
So here we are, in our made-up zendo on a made-up Rohatsu.
Zen Buddhists all over the world are doing the same thing.
This is the biggest, this is like the high holy days of Zen, the big occasion for the year.
The most formal way to celebrate a Rohatsu, maybe you already know, is you do like a sort of a seven-day and a little more sesshin.
You start on the first of December, and you do what we're doing today, but day after day for seven days.

Then on the evening of the seventh, you sit up all night, sit up all night to enact the central story of today: the story of Sakya Muni Buddha's enlightenment, which as you know, the story culminates, great heroic story, culminates in an epic night of all-night practice, or maybe those seven nights of practice.

I don't know, but there's a key final night when after working through many, many confusions and delusions and layers, this Buddha sort of finished waking up in the morning when he saw the morning star.

What's kind of great is we know that right now, this very moment in Zen temples and centers all over the world, people are sitting in sesshin, trying to touch their heart, trying to clarify their life.
We actually know one of these monks, Chris Burkhart, is right now at seven-day sesshin at Green Gulch Farm, like the fourth or fifth day of sesshin for her.
So we support her and we support all the other practitioners, and we are supported by them.

The story of Buddha's enlightenment, and the two thousand five hundred years on our calendar between now and that moment seemingly long ago, is also a story of lineage, story of ancestors, story of those who came before.
That long list of names, that's what that was, of course; you couldn't understand a single one of them, probably, but that's what that was.
It wasn't even just starting with Buddha.
Buddha was the eighth name on the list.
Before that were mythical Buddhas, even before that Buddha, because Indian time is not linear like ours; it's cyclical.
In the way Buddhism was understood in the beginning, there have been many ages with Buddhas, every age has a Buddha, and then they decline.
So it's a cyclical thing.
But we got to Buddha and we got to his first enlightened disciple, Mahakasyapa, Mahakasyodayosho, and his enlightened disciple, according to the Zen way of looking at things, Ananda Dayosho.
All the way down to Suzuki Roshi, who was the last name on the list, where we said Shogaku Shunyu Dayosho.
All Buddha schools emphasize lineage and ancestors to different extents.
Definitely all Buddhists honor and study certain key teachers in their lineage, reading and commenting over and over and over again on key works.
In a way, Buddhism is just sort of a continuous re-investigation and rediscovery of the same teachings, each generation seeing them in the way that they see them.
So there are books and teachings and history we can learn for sure.
But Zen Buddhism particularly strongly emphasizes a sort of lovely myth of student to teacher, generation after generation, in an unbroken line going back to Buddha.
That's the other symbolism of the list that we chanted.

They say that the teachings can't just be learned in a book; that they're outside words and letters, which is a teaching attributed to Bodhidharma, which was definitely made up in the eleventh century.
So that's how that can go.
But it's true, Bodhidharma also said it.
This is a powerful story, and it's practically and obviously true.
You have to meet other practitioners and work with teachers to really appreciate the possibilities and depth of practice.
They also say that Buddha's way can only be passed from warm hand to warm hand.
But like all stories and mythologies, it's also a little problematic.

One of the reasons why we don't chant that list every time we have early practice, besides the sort of bits of historical fiction that we know that are embedded in that list, the Indian ancestors are particularly suspect.
Early Buddhism in India, they didn't particularly think about things in terms of a linear lineage.
So the Chinese guys had to go back and reverse engineer.
It's also a list of men, of only men.
We know that from the time of Buddha, there were women practitioners, and so there's no way this could have been passed on without many women involved; it's not really possible.
So we could work hard to invent our own reverse engineer our own women's list of women too.
And they did that in a limited way at San Francisco Zen Center under Norman's supervision.
We will chant that list sometime too; that's equally made up and equally perfect, all these stories.
As we study the mind in zazen, we realize little by little that we too are just a story.
Why our story can be so difficult for us is we're not really in charge of it.
We're just one factor in the invention of our own story.
So we end up with very ungainly stories, personalities that we carry around with some things that we like embedded in them.
We seem to always get a personality with all these little things for sticking out that we don't like.
The little things that stick are sticking out of our personality seem to have a way of whacking into other people's little projections, resulting in a lot of suffering.
You might think that Zen practice is like a way that we could rub together and sort of smooth off all that stuff so we could just be shining, graceful, beautiful Buddha beings.
That's true in a way; it's true in a way.
Practice does help us.
But in another way, it's not true at all.
This personality, this container, was created by conditions far beyond our control.
These tendencies that we have that bother us, we will definitely have until we die and maybe lifetimes after that.

What Zen practice can do so beautifully, and I think is its most important contribution to human life, is it can help us shift our attitude and understanding of this spiky personality that we have to carry around.
We can understand our tendencies and our unwholesome problematic qualities as just the conditions of our life, as just the hand we were dealt, ours to work with as best we can.
We can absolutely remove the incredible amount of extra energy and suffering and anguish and guilt and disturbance that we add on top of all that.
When we bump into people with our little spiky parts, we can learn to say we're sorry, to understand a little more clearly, and let it go.
We can really change the context of our life, and we can experience this directly through zazen practice and through sesshin practice.
We can really see the way it goes with mind and conditions and who we think we are.
It's real hard.
I feel like I'm stumbling a little bit.
It's hard to quite explain this with words.
Maybe you know what I'm talking about anyway.
Zazen practice is not going to fix you, because that you is not a you that can or should be fixed.
But zazen practice can support you in understanding more clearly the nature of this being and this living, and then it's not such a problem.
Anyway, let's talk about Buddha.
That's what you're supposed to do.
Sorry, that was a long description.

That was a long side road there.

He really can't go on with his life the way he's been living it.
He has to abandon everything and begin his heroic journey, leaving home to do nothing but spiritual practice until he could figure out how could anybody live?

So he did that.
Time after time, meeting a teacher, practicing very assiduously in a very smart, skillful way, like he's the best student, you know.
He is like the ideal practitioner, time after time mastering the teachings of each teacher.

How could it be that he would just one day in a couple of days get sick and die and be gone?
How can that make any sense?
And how can we go about our business like everything's fine?
Everything is not fine.

Then he said, then I thought he remembered something.

Very still.
